prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The equipment fills the upper-left/central foreground at roughly 0.2–0.8 m, the camera wearer’s forearms and hands are about 0.3–0.7 m away below it, and the detached wheel lies to the right on the floor at roughly 0.8–1.5 m; another person’s partly cropped legs are beyond the equipment, approximately 1–2 m away. The depth ordering makes the close machine surfaces and arms stand out from the darker, more distant floor, and shows that the wheel is farther from the wearer than the controls but near the other person’s feet. Across the five frames the viewpoint turns or shifts rightward around the equipment: the wheel moves from lower-right toward upper-right and the visible arms change position, while the equipment remains within the wearer’s arm’s reach and continues to occlude much of the person beyond it. Absolute metre estimates are uncertain because this is uncalibrated monocular depth, and several machine boundaries, arms, legs, and the wheel have flattened or inconsistent brightness that makes exact separations and motion unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks expose coarse foreground regions and occlusion boundaries, especially where the camera wearer’s arms overlap the equipment and where the cropped standing person appears behind it near the top edge. They suggest multiple person-like regions around the central and right portions of the strip, generally within about 0.3–2 m of the wearer and separated from one another by the equipment and roughly 0.5–1.5 m, but they do not support dependable distances, facing direction, gaze, or above/below ordering beyond visible mask placement. Across the frames, person-shaped regions and the large equipment region shift laterally as the viewpoint turns, with several bodies remaining partly outside the top and right edges; the wearer’s hands remain near the machine, while the distant person regions stay beyond it. The map is highly unreliable: the equipment is labelled “motorcycle,” wheel/background areas are labelled “frisbee” or “person,” several masks cover large empty regions, and identities fragment or disappear between frames, so many apparent people and objects are false detections.
descriptions.pose: The pose map primarily localizes magenta hand keypoints: hand clusters appear near the middle of frames 2–4 at approximately 0.3–0.8 m in the RGB context, and a larger hand appears high on the right in frame 5 at roughly 0.3–0.7 m. These keypoints clarify finger and hand orientation against the visually cluttered dark equipment, showing hands beside or above machine parts and therefore within arm’s reach, while the fifth-frame hand is raised near the upper-right edge and partly cropped. The hand clusters move rightward and change orientation across the sequence, consistent with relative hand motion and/or a rightward camera turn, but no stable yellow body skeleton is visible to establish full-body position, person-to-person spacing, facing direction, or gaze. Missing detections in frame 1, disconnected or duplicate-looking hand traces, and the absence of limbs and torsos make approach, retreat, occlusion, and ownership of each detected hand uncertain.
